title: What University Licensors Should Learn From TexasLDPC v. Broadcom - Crowell & Moring LLP
content:
Universities should closely review patent licenses granted to startups. When a university licenses its patents to a startup for commercialization, revenue generation, and market entry, what happens if the startup runs out of capital and shifts its focus exclusively to enforcing and monetizing the licensed patents? The Federal Circuit’s decision in TexasLDPC Inc. v. Broadcom Inc. offers important guidance.  The license must specify what constitutes business operations within the meaning of automatic termination clause in operative terms, not merely in recitals. License or Assignment. If a university grants a licensee an exclusive license together with the sole and exclusive right to enforce the patents, the arrangement is effectively an assignment and gives the licensee standing to sue without joining the university. TexasLDPC held an exclusive license to patents developed at Texas A&M University. After years of attempting to commercialize the underlying technology, TexasLDPC exhausted its capital and shifted its business entirely to patent enforcement, eventually filing infringement suits against Broadcom and its affiliates. The district court dismissed the case on two grounds. First, the district court concluded that TexasLDPC had “ceased its business operations” within the meaning of the agreement’s automatic termination clause by abandoning commercialization and development, thereby extinguishing the license and TexasLDPC’s standing to sue. Second, the district court dismissed for failure to join Texas A&M as a necessary party. The Federal Circuit reversed on both grounds. On the termination issue, the court held that the agreement unambiguously contemplated enforcement as one of TexasLDPC’s “business operations”—not merely an ancillary activity. The court pointed to several operative provisions: one provision granting co-equal rights to use, to sublicense, and to sue for infringement without elevating one right above the others; the definition of “commercially reasonable efforts” expressly including enforcement; and another provision barring termination so long as the licensee was exercising commercially reasonable enforcement efforts. Because these operative clauses were unambiguous, the court held that the agreement’s recitals could not override the operative provisions. The Federal Circuit further held that the agreement conveyed “all substantial rights” in the patents to TexasLDPC, entitling it to sue for infringement in its own name without joining Texas A&M as a co-plaintiff. The result: the license survived despite the termination clause’s focus on “business operations” because other license provisions contemplated enforcement as a business operation, even if it “abandoned efforts to further develop the technology or sublicense” the IP.  For universities, the lesson is clear: whether the intent is to permit enforcement as a standalone business activity or to limit the license to practicing entities, the agreement must say so in operative terms—silence or reliance on aspirational recitals will not suffice in either direction. The TexasLDPC ruling makes clear that universities should expressly define what counts as “business operations” under a patent license. If the institution intends to require continued commercialization or development of the licensed technology, the agreement should say so directly. A general termination clause tied to “business operations,” without more, may not be enough to prevent a licensee from arguing that patent enforcement alone satisfies that requirement. Universities should therefore address an important threshold issue at the drafting stage: must the licensee continue developing or commercializing the technology, or is patent enforcement and monetization also an acceptable use of the license? The answer should appear in the operative provisions of the agreement—not only in recitals or preamble language. As TexasLDPC illustrates, statements in “whereas” clauses about commercialization and development were insufficient to override operative provisions that treated enforcement as a co-equal right. The district court relied heavily on the agreement’s “whereas” clauses, which referenced the licensor’s “desire to commercialize the intellectual property for the public benefit and welfare” and the licensee’s “expertise in commercialization and development,” to conclude that enforcement was at most an ancillary activity. The Federal Circuit rejected that approach entirely. The Federal Circuit held that those recitals were “of such a broad and generic quality” that they could not override the agreement’s operative provisions, which explicitly contemplated enforcement as both a right and a means of satisfying contractual milestones. The lesson is straightforward: if commercialization is a condition of the deal, it must appear in the operative clauses, not merely in the preamble. Non-operative preamble and recitals set context; they do not govern rights. The ruling’s second major holding is equally significant. The Federal Circuit found that TexasLDPC’s exclusive right to make, use, and sell licensed products, combined with its “first and only right to enforce” the patents against third parties, transferred all substantial rights and sufficient to confer standing to sue for infringement without joining Texas A&M as a co-plaintiff. For universities, this raises a critical structuring question: how much enforcement autonomy should a licensee have? The answer shapes not only the university’s litigation exposure but also the practical question of whether the university retains meaningful oversight over how its intellectual property is deployed in enforcement proceedings. Universities that wish to preserve control over enforcement decisions and to ensure alignment between the licensee’s activities and the university’s institutional objectives must structure their license grants with that outcome in mind. title: Endorsement: Reject San Mateo Community College District’s $848 million Measure V - The Mercury News

The San Mateo County Community College District is asking voters to approve an $848 million bond program to repair and upgrade facilities on its three campuses. To sell Measure V, the district deceptively claims that the measure would not increase property owners’ “current tax rates.” And campaign signs for the measure falsely state that it would support community colleges “without raising taxes.” Making matters worse, the district doesn’t have a concrete plan for how it would spend the borrowed money, much of which would not be available for more than a decade. Voters should not stand for such deception and ambiguity. They should reject Measure V. District property owners are still paying extra taxes to retire the debt from about $1 billion of bonds voters approved in 2001, 2005 and 2014. Those annual taxes, which currently total about $18 for every $100,000 of assessed value, work out to about $216 a year for a home with a median assessed value of $1.2 million. That $18 tax rate is projected to decline rapidly starting in 2031 as the current bonds are paid off. But if Measure V passes, the district would issue more bonds and schedule the repayments to start as the existing bonds are paid off. The result is that the tax would extend the annual rate of $18 per $100,000 of assessed value for another 17 years, until 2048. It’s a charade to claim that’s not a tax increase. Property owners would be paying more taxes over a longer period of time. It would be more transparent to call the measure a 17-year tax extension. Meanwhile, to keep the tax rate the same, the district must delay issuing bonds. Nearly half the total would not be issued until 2036 and 2038, at which time the district’s needs could be completely different from today. And the measure would allow the district board to completely change its plans for the money. In other words, voters today won’t know what they’re buying by approving Measure V. The legal language of Measure V lists possible projects, like modernizing the Cañada College fine arts building, the College of San Mateo gym and the Skyline College Kinesiology and Wellness Center. But there’s no clarity as to when or in what order the projects would be completed, assuming plans don’t change first. The list also includes $180 million for construction of 165,000 square feet of new student housing at Cañada and Skyline. That works out to about $1,100 a square foot. The details are thin. District officials told us they would want to pair the money with state funding, but they were unclear on whether state money would be available. Moreover, there’s no mention of student housing in the ballot language or impartial analysis that voters might read. The housing is only mentioned deep in the measure’s legal language. Student housing is an unusual investment for an urban community college district. It’s questionable whether that would be the best use of limited construction funds. What we have is a ballot measure that hides the amount and nature of the tax increase to pay for an indeterminate list of projects, half of which won’t begin for at least 10 years. Voters deserve more transparency, specificity and foresight. content: The Final of The Great Conquest, which will take place on Saturday 21 November at Estadio Metropolitano Roberto Meléndez in Barranquilla, will bring together two clubs with a rich history and extensive experience in continental competition. Almost half a century separates their first meeting in South American competition from the 2026 CONMEBOL Sudamericana Final. The Xeneize, champions in 2003 and 2004, will face Eduardo Domínguez's side — runners-up in the previous edition of the competition — in a showdown for another major trophy to add to their already impressive collections. Boca reached the semi-finals as the reigning champions. Juan Carlos Lorenzo's side secured an important 2-1 win at the Mineirão, with Miguel Ángel Bordón scoring twice and Marcelo Oliveira pulling one back for the hosts. The second leg at La Bombonera also went the Argentine side's way, as Boca won 3-1 thanks to goals from Ernesto Mastrángelo, Toninho Cerezo (an own goal) and Carlos Salinas. Marinho had briefly brought the scores level in the first half. The result sent Boca through to the Final, where they defeated Deportivo Cali to lift their second CONMEBOL Libertadores title. So far, the only time the two clubs have contested a South American title against each other was in the 1993 edition of the Copa de Oro. The tie was closely fought: the first leg in Belo Horizonte ended 0-0, before Boca claimed a 1-0 win at La Bombonera in the return fixture, with defender Carlos Mac Allister scoring a header. Seven years later, the sides met again in the quarter-finals of the Copa Mercosur, where the Brazilian team secured their first win against Boca Juniors. In Belo Horizonte, Galo won 2-0 through goals from Marques and Argentine forward Diego Capria. The second leg in Buenos Aires ended 2-2, sending Mineiro through with a 4-2 aggregate victory. Antonio Barijho scored both of Boca's goals under Carlos Bianchi, while Cláudio Caçapa and André Neles found the net for the visitors. Their most recent meeting came in the Round of 16 of the 2021 CONMEBOL Libertadores. The 180 minutes of normal time ended goalless, and the tie was decided on penalties in Belo Horizonte, with the Brazilian side winning 3-1. Éverson was the standout performer in goal for the Minas Gerais club that night: he saved Esteban Rolón's spot-kick before scoring his own — the final kick of the shoot-out — past Agustín Rossi. The head-to-head record between the clubs remains finely balanced. Although one side won the only title they have contested against each other, the other has come out on top in their two most recent knockout ties. Barranquilla will provide the setting for another chapter in the Boca Juniors–Atlético Mineiro rivalry, an unmissable football occasion that will crown a new continental champion.

title: Rosemary V. St. Aubin - The Post-Crescent
content: Rosemary Veda St. Aubin (née Meinert), age 96, passed away peacefully in Kaukauna, Wisconsin, on October 25, 2026. Born in Kaukauna, Rosemary graduated from Kaukauna High School and went on to earn a Bachelor of Music degree from Lawrence College in Appleton. For more than five decades, she served as an organist and choir director at St. John Catholic Church in Little Chute and Our Savior’s Lutheran Church in Appleton. She also shared her musical talents at countless funerals, weddings, and Masses, and passed along her love of the piano to hundreds of students through private lessons. In the early 1970s, Rosemary returned to college to earn her teaching certification and subsequently worked as a substitute music teacher in Fox Valley schools. Rosemary will be remembered for her deep love of family, especially her cherished grandchildren. She took great pride in her German heritage, sharing traditional dishes and homemade baked goods, particularly her much-loved overnight buns. A talented and devoted seamstress and needleworker, she created beautiful textile heirlooms that will be treasured by her family for generations. Rosemary is survived by her five children: Louis, Laurie (Eric), Jessica Jacobs (Bruce), Lee (Lynn), and Joel (Shannon); seven grandchildren: Eli, Emma Mannino (Carmelo), Kyle (Mickenzie), Elizabeth Knepper (Brendan), Benjamin Jacobs, Khloe, and Karsyn; and eight great-grandchildren. She is also survived by numerous nieces and nephews, including her very special niece, Mary Britten, whose kindness, patience, and devotion were deeply appreciated by Rosemary and her entire family. Rosemary was preceded in death by her beloved husband, Roger; her parents, Ferdinand and Beatrice Meinert; and her siblings, Collette Vargo, Jerome (Georgie) Meinert, and Kenneth (Aura) Meinert. The family extends its heartfelt gratitude to Rosemary’s caregivers from Right at Home, especially Julie, and to the staff of St. Paul Home and Hospice for their compassionate care, kindness, and support. A Mass of Christian Burial will be celebrated on Thursday, November 5, 2026, at 3:00 p.m. at St. Katharine Drexel Parish, St. Mary’s Church, 119 W. 7th Street, Kaukauna, with Fr. Luke Ferris officiating. Family and friends are invited to gather at the church beginning at 2:00 p.m., prior to the service. Rosemary will be laid to rest at St. John Catholic Cemetery in Little Chute. In lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made to St. Paul Elder Services or St. Katharine Drexel Parish, both in Kaukauna. Coping with grief when a traditional funeral isn't possible

title: Five Things We Learned From Liverpool v Chelsea In The Carabao Cup - Yahoo Sports
content: Liverpool advanced into the Quarter-Final stage of the Carabao Cup, edging past a stubborn Chelsea side on penalties. The two sides were very evenly matched, with the only goals of the game coming from the penalty spot. Morgan Rogers and Cody Gakpo both converted spot kicks in the first half, and the second half was scrappy and lacking quality in the final third from either side. What followed was a rollercoaster penalty shootout that resulted in a Reds victory. Here are five things we learned from this successful cup tie. The Georgian goalkeeper was outstanding for the Reds, especially during the latter stages of the game. While Mamardashvili's distribution was questionable at times, his shot-stopping prowess was clear for all to see. A crucial save late in the game to deny Chelsea a winner, before saving a penalty in the shootout that ultimately secured Liverpool's place in the quarter-finals. The three up front for Liverpool had all previously played together; however, the positions/roles that they were all assigned left many scratching their heads. Rather than playing Lewis Koumas through the middle of the three, he featured on the right-hand side. Rio Ngumoha started on the left, and Cody Gakpo played up front. Perhaps this was an attempt to add some physicality against a three-at-the-back Chelsea defence, but Gakpo was no match for the physical dominance that the likes of Fofana and Lacroix were able to produce. Many fans are running out of superlatives to describe Ronald Araujo this season, and against Chelsea, he was once again vital in securing the win. Playing in his more natural centre-back role, the Uruguayan was immense, winning several key aerial duels as well as making some thunderous challenges. He came off the bench against Villarreal and changed the game for Liverpool, and he had a very similar impact against the Blues. While a goal wasn't scored while he was on the pitch, Iraola's side played a lot better when the German entered the fray. A big hurdle has been overcome in defeating Chelsea, with Manchester City now the only traditional "top six side" left in the tournament, other than Liverpool. A cup win early in Andoni Iraola's reign at the club would be huge, something he has gone on record and said himself. But now a difficult task awaits in the quarter-final as Bournemouth will travel to Anfield and fight for a spot in the semi-finals. title: The Most Chilling Details About V for Vendetta’s Future - Consequence of Sound
content: Log in to track artists, discover shows, and stay in the loop. By continuing, you agree to the terms & conditions. Director James McTeigue reflects on the background details which make the movie feel far too relevant today The dystopian thriller V for Vendetta, based on the graphic novel by writer Alan Moore and artist David Lloyd, is currently celebrating its 20th anniversary with a special theatrical re-release. But it still proves chilling today because of how familiar so many of its most disturbing moments feel. It’s something director James McTeigue acknowledges in a new interview with Consequence: “The tools of any government that leans authoritarian are the same. The things that Alan Moore discussed during the Thatcherite period, we discussed during the Bush period, and you could discuss now. The fear of otherness, the endless war, the fear of immigration. All the things that are in [V for Vendetta] are happening at this moment. You can watch the movie then, and you can watch it now, and it’s completely resonant to what is happening.” As fans of the source material, the Wachowskis first began writing the script for V for Vendetta in the 1990s, prior to the smash success of The Matrix. According to McTeigue, the initial draft he saw was 170 pages long — the common math for screenplays is that one page equals one minute of screen time, so that was clearly a bit long for a commercial film in the mid-2000s. Thus, further drafts dropped some subplots and honed in on a central narrative: a young woman (Natalie Portman) and a masked vigilante (Hugh Weaving) fighting back against the oppressive rule of High Chancellor Adam Sutler (John Hurt) and his fascist government. What wasn’t lost in the adaptation process was the comic’s rich array of details in the background. McTeigue and the filmmaking team didn’t hold back in creating a totalitarian London: Throughout the film, photographs of Sutler are visible in the homes of many citizens, while propaganda posters featuring slogans like “Strength Through Unity/Unity Through Faith” are seen on walls. Scrolling digital displays remind citizens of curfew hours and other important government messages. The all-seeing government feels like a tangible force throughout. “If you look really hard, you’ll see a bunch of stuff in there that you probably don’t notice on the first viewing or the second viewing,” McTeigue says. “There’s lots of stuff in the background.” Something the team found freeing was the fact that V for Vendetta takes place in a nebulous near-future. (The graphic novel begins in the year 1997, but the movie’s timeline is much vaguer.) “You can put old things in there, and new things, things that you haven’t seen before,” McTeigue says. Another benefit was that McTeigue had a good shorthand with production designer Owen Paterson, who he’d met even before prior to collaborating together on The Matrix films. (McTeigue was second unit/assistant director on the sci-fi classic.) Together, they created something that spoke to McTeigue’s aim, with his first film, to execute it similarly to “the first album concept. It was 35 years of everything that I’ve liked about politics and music and film all put into this one movie.” This desire emerges most powerfully in the sequences that take place in V’s home base (known as the Shadow Gallery) and a secret archive of art hoarded by closeted talk show host Gordon Deitrich (Stephen Fry). Both spaces are packed with artwork and other artifacts on display — leading to the dark realization that even innocuous things like an old movie posters are hidden there because there is no place for them in this heavily restrictive society. As McTeigue notes, “Okay, if the government has this list of objectionable materials, what is that? What paintings? What photographs, what music, what sculptures? We discussed all that with the set dresser, Peter Walpole.” Like so many authoritarian governments, those in power in this world believe firmly in “the suppression of minorities.” Hence these exhibits include photography by Robert Mapplethorpe alongside banned art by Francis Bacon and other subversive works: “Stuff that was made by and for the so-called people who are ‘other.’ Because otherness is the thing that authoritarian governments go after.” There are also fictional creations on display in both the Shadow Gallery and Deitrich’s secret room, such as a movie poster for The Salt Flats, a movie starring a doomed actress whose story Evey learns during her imprisonment. Many other pieces were fabricated for rights issues, or in order to fit into this fictional world. One of the more eye-catching examples in Deitrich’s collection is a large graphic print referencing Jamie Reid’s infamous album cover for The Sex Pistols’ God Save the Queen. The twist is that instead of the Queen, it features John Hurt in character as Sutler, wearing a crown — clearly created by a subversive artist protesting the current government. McTeigue says that he did not actually ask Hurt to wear a crown for the print — it was added to a photograph of him later. But he does think that Hurt would have done so if requested. “He was funny, Johnny — he was a great guy. And he did a great job — he’s so ridiculous as Sutler. I wanted him to be over the top… Of course, I thought I was going over the top then, but there’s no way I can compare him to politicians of now, and how ridiculous and over the top they are.” That leads again to the most haunting aspect of V for Vendetta — how relevant it all is to today. McTeigue attributes this to the idea of there being “cycles” in international politics. “You have a good cycle, you have a bad cycle. It doesn’t really matter what side of the political spectrum you’re on, you can see it for what it is.” Although McTeigue does believe that we’ll get out of this cycle eventually, “because we always do,” he acknowledges that “maybe it’s been more insidious this time around.” Endemic to the mess we’re currently in, he points out, is gaslighting — something depicted frequently in V for Vendetta, such as the government response to V blowing up the old Bailey. “You know, what I say is white, you say is black… I think if you take a step back, you can see the ridiculousness of it if you care to look underneath the surface. You can see that there is this constant lying that goes on, and that baseline of truth has disappeared out the window for the next little while.” Even if the movie stands out as a too-real reflection of today, McTeigue thinks that the movie’s central message remains an optimistic one. “That’s the Evie story, right? She goes through hell for what she believes, but comes out at the end of it with hope.” That, and the fact that historically the “bad cycles” have not lasted forever, keep him from feeling completely helpless. You have to have hope, he says, because “otherwise you’d feel like you had an 80-pound anvil pressing down on the back of your neck every day.” There’s another message from the movie that McTeigue takes comfort in: Governments should be afraid of their people. “I think that’s true. They should be, right?” he says. “I think when the disparity between the working people and the people who are in power becomes too much, that there’s power in numbers.” Or, to put it in 2026 terms: “All those tech bros should be careful about what they wish for.” V for Vendetta returns to theaters for its 20th anniversary on November 1st and 5th, thanks to Fathom Entertainment. title: Priyanka Chopra Jonas, V Join Andrew Scott on Short 'We Were Here' - Variety
content:
Priyanka Chopra Jonas and Tony-winning activist-playwright V, formerly known as Eve Ensler, have signed on as executive producers of Pranav Bhasin’s Oscar-qualified Indian short “We Were Here.” They join Andrew Scott as the film gears up for awards season. The New Yorker has acquired the short and will premiere it on the magazine’s YouTube channels. “We Were Here” has screened at more than 80 festivals and collected over 20 awards. It launched at the Clermont-Ferrand International Short Film Festival, taking the Canal+ Prize. At SXSW, it won the audience award for best narrative short along with the Redbreast Unhidden Award. Palm Springs International ShortFest named it best live-action short under 15 minutes and best comedy short, and that win made the film eligible for Academy Award consideration. Bhasin wrote and directed the mockumentary, set in a small Indian town. Three retirees, certain that machines are stealing human jobs, mount a protest by posing as household appliances. Their campaign is thrown off course when one of their children goes to work for an artificial intelligence company. Satish Kashyap, Devendra Dodke and Arindol Bagchi star as Mr. Bagchi, Mr. Pimple and Mr. Ganguli. The cast also includes Shubham Kujur, Kalpana Gagdekar and Yash Gonsai. Gonsai produced through Sunshine Pictures alongside Dheer Momaya and Dar Gai. Aarti Lohia and SPLF Media present the film. Lohia serves as an executive producer on the project. “This film offers a refreshing, witty take on a subject that feels very timely. I jumped at the opportunity to come on board as an executive producer to amplify this creative team and ensure their brilliant, original vision gets the spotlight it deserves,” said Chopra Jonas. The executive producer roster also includes Peter S. Kim and Nalini Sharma of Basement Video, Neha Kaul, Megha Kadakia, Priya Giri Desai and Shruti Ganguly of Prism Entertainment, Shivani Pandya Malhotra, Film Companion Studios, Anjula Acharia and Pan Nalin. Devaiah Bopanna, Earlyman Film, Rahul Bharti, Supavitra Babul and Vaibhav Bundhoo are co-producers. Bhasin, who hails from Mumbai, was directing films by the age of 13 and had made his first series, for TVF, by 17. At the Mumbai film festival, his short “Wolf of Chawl Street” took the Silver Dimensions prize in 2017, and “New Year’s Eve” was named best short a year later. His other work includes “Taylor’s Version” and “Screaming on the Fly.” His films have premiered at SXSW and on Mubi, Short of the Week and Vimeo Staff Picks. He is an alumnus of Vanishing Angle’s Short-to-Feature Lab (2020) and the Zurich Film Festival Academy (2022). “‘We Were Here’ started as a small, silly idea about three uncles trying to stop the spread of AI, and somewhere along the way, I fell in love with them, their friendships, and their stubborn resilience. In India, reality is often stranger than anything you could write, and the mockumentary format let me keep the film rooted in real people and real places, while exploring just how absurd things can get,” said Bhasin. “Now that the film is Oscar-qualified, I’m still figuring out how to process it. I made it the way I make everything. I followed an idea that felt wild to me, all the way to the end. I was never sure it would make sense to anyone outside my head. As a young filmmaker, I find it pretty surreal to have a tribe of highly accomplished and committed EPs, including Andrew Scott, Priyanka Chopra Jonas, and V. We’re all really excited to find creative ways to get this film to wider audiences.” Gonsai was an executive producer on Nalin’s “Last Film Show,” which made the international feature shortlist at the 95th Academy Awards. He more recently teamed with Dharma Productions on Neeraj Ghaywan’s Cannes-debuting “Homebound,” which was shortlisted at the 98th Academy Awards. 0 Comments Comments are moderated. title: 2027 Honda HR-V Review: Practical, Slow, Not as Cool as the Fit It Replaced - The Drive
content:
Published				

					Oct 29, 2026 10:00 AM EDT The Daily Brief wraps up the biggest stories and our exclusive reporting on the auto industry and car culture. The 2027 Honda HR-V is the sort of car that doesn’t demand much of the driver. So as I cruised down the highway behind the wheel of my tester, I got to thinking about what this car actually is and how it came to be. That journey led me to a sobering realization: At 3,150 pounds (3,275 with all-wheel drive), this is what passes for a “small” Honda in 2026. Dang. Fundamentally, the HR-V started out as a punched-out Honda Fit, but it absolutely dwarfs the old hatchback. Sure, the Fit grew slightly before being somewhat unceremoniously killed off here in the United States, but it’s hard to believe the HR-V ever shared any DNA with Honda’s subcompact. The HR-V is based on the Civic architecture, and consequently it’s taller, roomier, and even comes with all-wheel drive. If you’re familiar with the outgoing model year, the 2027 HR-V will be old hat—nothing’s changed. This generation hit the market in 2022 as a ’23 model, so it’s due for an update. Perhaps next year? The design may be a bit long in the tooth, especially for something that looked kind of like a half-melted Ford Escape to begin with, but in small-car circles, form typically follows function. The HR-V’s generous size brings plenty of interior room and a decent cargo area. If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it, right? While the HR-V’s interior leans more toward bland than minimalist, the Civic-esque details work well enough, and the basic interfaces are handled by perfectly intuitive knobs and switches. Physical controls for the win. Under the hood, there’s a 2.0-liter, 158-horsepower four-cylinder that produces 138 pound-feet of torque at 4,200 RPM. A continuously variable transmission sends power to either the front wheels or all four. When the HR-V first hit the market, you could skip the power-sucking CVT and option the front-wheel-drive model with a manual. In that guise, it almost felt zippy. Almost. This? Calling this all-wheel-drive EX-L a dog would insult geriatric, three-legged canines everywhere. Few cars make my 3.8-liter Wrangler feel fast, and this is one of them. You could put it in the bed of a Ridgeline, and the truck would still probably hit 60 mph quicker than the HR-V on its own. Still, I have a soft spot for it. It won’t scratch the enthusiast itch, but it’s both surprisingly quiet (even on the highway, where Hondas once struggled with wind and tire roar) and comfortable. The EX-L’s wheel/tire combination is spot-on for battered urban roads. It’s a bit soft in the corners, I’ll readily admit, but it rides like a dream, and the wheel is still plenty responsive despite the lack of feedback. There’s a lot to like about the 2027 Honda HR-V, but it’s also simply a lot of car. That may look good on paper, but for some (including me), Honda lost something when it translated its subcompact hatchback into a small SUV. Is this what the market wants? Perhaps, but it’s hard to accept knowing what we sacrificed to get it. Honda provided The Drive with a 7-day loan of this vehicle for the purpose of writing this review.
